newsitem.title: USA: ALPINE SKIING-WOMEN'S WORLD CUP RACE THREATENED BY WEATHER.
newsitem.headline: ALPINE SKIING-WOMEN'S WORLD CUP RACE THREATENED BY WEATHER.

text.p: Already marred by a season-ending injury to world champion Picabo Street, Friday's second World Cup downhill women's race of the season faces a threat from snowstorms.

A storm front sweeping across the Colorado Rockies poses a potential hazard for the a race which lost a major element of interest Wednesday when Street, the tour's downhill winner the past two seasons and reigning world champion, was injured in a training crash.

Falling heavily near the finish, Street skidded hard into a retaining fence. Dr Richard Steadman, U.S. ski team physician, diagnosed the injury as a complete tear of the anterior cruciate ligament. He will perform surgery next week when the swelling subsides.
Street finished fourth in the season opener last weekend at Lake Louise, Canada, won by Katja Seizinger of Germany.
"It's sad that Picabo is hurt, but there are lots of other racers to compete against," said Seizinger, who won on this same course in 1992 and 1994.
The list would include France's surging Carole Montillet and Sweden's Pernilla Wiberg, second and third in the opener, and Russian powerhouse Warwara Zelenskaja, frequently among the leaders.

Street and Seizinger finished 1-2 in the downhill standings last season, when Seizinger captured her first overall title. Their downhill duels were anticipated as a highlight of the season. Seizinger won three straight titles, 1992-94, before Street began her current run.
This Vail event has been the busiest on the women's schedule, with seven races since 1991, and Seizinger has been most successful.
A speed specialist when she began her World Cup career in 1990, the 24-year-old has evolved as its strongest all-around skier, winning the season giant slalom opener as well.

Seizinger again has the overall lead with 305 points, although Wiberg stamps herself a worthy challenger at 258. Finally fully recovered from her injuries, the Swede has a dual goal this season: to win a downhill race and capture the overall title.

"I've never done either of those things and it's something to aim for," said Wiberg, whose eight-year career includes five Olympic and world championship medals. "This is a wonderful beginning for me."
Wednesday's first training run, conducted in gusting winds following an overnight snowfall, produced slower times than usual.
"The course seemed very easy," Seizinger said, "but that changes every day.''
The two-event Vail programme concludes Saturday with super-G.
